note:
[Vivek Chibber]'s interview on Doomscroll.

Some points that [Chibber] makes:

* Academia and NGOs control the left now
* Management, Academia, NGOs (MANGOs) have shifted primarily towards identity politics
* The current left's focus is on career building and seeking notoriety, focused on talking about identity politics, instead of consensus building, confronting capital or otherwise talking about class and building coalitions
* This leads to political/revolutionary tourism, where people can join groups ostensibly about building coalitions but can derail the goals by focusing on their hobby horse then leave without having to face the repercussions 
* Current left has contempt for the poor, considering them racist, misogynist, trans-phobes, etc and end up wearing their inability to convince coalitions as a merit badge instead of a failure to make progress
* Compare with Togliatti in the 1930s who fled to Russia from Italy, where Togliatti is grappling with how they failed to win over workers so that they flocked to Mussolini, with the current left that instead considers it a failure on the masses part, rather anything they've done to not win them over
* Current left has no possibility to win and have no incentive to change because their motivation is for personal advancement or satisfaction, rather than change
* Talks about sociologists in academia now are escaping the job market, contrasted with 30 years ago, who were mostly trying to do research and good. It's not clear which other academic disciplines this transfers over to
* The moral collapse of radicalism is to be career focused, focusing on career advancement through high impact journal publication, and making sure to adopt the worldview and language for that career advancement while not actually challenging power, so as not to jeopardize their career advancement
* The professional managerial class (PMC) that would traditionally go into industry now goes into academia, bringing their focus on career advancement and accumulation of power, while supporting the status quo and suppressing any radicalism that would provide a serious challenge to power
* "[The PMC] want a radicalism that's consistent with their career ambitions"
* "Radicalism now becomes a radicalism that uses the language of oppression, domination, and justice ... and refashions the goals of liberation to the impediments ... to upward mobility"
* By turning the focus from empowering workers and the poor to oppression, and since oppression is everywhere, the fight can be localized to your immediate vicinity, in particular the impediments to your upward mobility in white collar and academic jobs, without the need to displace yourself to where exploitation of workers and the poor is. Refusing to place a hierarchy on oppression or exploitation means oppression locally can be elevated to equal to mass exploitation and gives a rationalization of why the local fight for personal gain is just as important as the oppression or exploitation elsewhere
* " 'Wherever you are, fight there.' It sounds great but the fact is that the places you inhabit may not be at all be important in the reproduction of the key forms of domination in society."
* The cultural turn is the idea that they key to understanding society and changing it is to focus on culture rather than focus on economics
* Claims that there was a turn in the 1980s where instead of admitting that people's material circumstances are the overwhelming issue but understand that they interpret them through a cultural prism, that, instead, the philosophy changed to believe that culture makes people's world
* The Foucauldian turn (multiple oppression theory aka intersectionality): ideas of power are outdated ("hangover from 19th century philosophy") and that the "intercises" are the key, that is power everywhere and all the time, so that fighting everywhere is the response
* "As long you're taking radicalism to be the fight against disparities, you're golden because disparities will never end.  ... Which means for the professional classes ... [will be] fights within the top 2% of the population over who gets what while burning down the other 98%"
* "The kind of capitalism we're facing is also very different ... It's no longer a capitalism that's based in the advanced world ... with the manufacturing industries. It's a service-based and a much more of a financial capitalism."

One point I take issue with is [Chibber]'s talk about a green component of any political movement, to curtail climate change, for example. [Chibber] says:

> Whatever your goals are for the environmental movement
> it's going to require taking on big sectors of the existing business community,
> obviously fossil fuels, but also others.
> .. To do that, you're going to have to have some kind of leverage to bring them to heel.
> ... Historically, the only sector of society that's had the power to bring business to heel
> has been labor.

I'm not confident about my belief but this seems to be missing the forest for the trees a bit. This ignores technological advances that have empowered people, labor included, to be able to push back against nodes of power. In particular, fossil fuel energy companies might be completely neutered by solar and battery deployment to satisfy energy needs. One can imagine either a soft revolution where fossil fuel companies fade into irrelevancy or, if there is a confrontation, labor is emboldened by a foundation of solar and battery energy to make demands.

One other point is that [Chibber] looks to admit that central planning is almost surely doomed to failure. It sounds like there are some intellectuals in socialist spheres that understand this and that ideas of some type of marriage of free markets with socialism have been considered.
